RCS is defined as the ratio of scattered power density to incident power density at a specified range under far-field conditions.
Far-field criteria require the target to be at least 2D²/λ away from the radar, where D is the largest target dimension and λ is the wavelength.
Monostatic RCS requires specification of two angular coordinates, while bistatic RCS requires four.
Polarization components in RCS measurements include principal (co-polarized) and cross-polarized terms, typically denoted as u_hh, u_vv, u_hv, and u_vh.
Dimensional scaling uses frequency and size scaling to maintain electromagnetic similarity, enabling smaller-scale measurements.
Long targets require very large ranges to satisfy far-field conditions due to space loss variations along their length.
Early RCS measurements used narrow-band CW waveforms; modern systems use wide-bandwidth waveforms for higher resolution.
Dynamic RCS measurements simulate target motion and clutter environments, unlike static isolated target measurements.
Advances in solid-state electronics and digital processing have greatly enhanced RCS measurement capabilities and accuracy.
Fourier transform techniques help isolate target scattering from facility clutter and improve measurement resolution.
RCS depends strongly on target geometry, material properties, orientation, radar frequency, waveform, and polarization.
Calibration standards are essential to reference RCS measurements to absolute levels.
Measurement accuracy is limited by polarization purity, multipath effects, and instrumentation sensitivity.
The scattering matrix approach allows transformation between polarization bases (e.g., linear to circular).
RCS is often expressed in dBsm (decibels relative to one square meter) for logarithmic representation.
Target depolarization effects are caused by asymmetry, roughness, and material properties.
Radar waveform processing influences the observed RCS, especially with high-resolution and Doppler processing.
Measurement facilities include outdoor ranges, anechoic chambers, and compact ranges for different frequency bands.
The RCS of rotationally symmetric targets viewed along the symmetry axis shows null cross-polarized responses.
Repetition of measurements at different ranges helps verify far-field conditions and measurement consistency.
